en: Notes on the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, Fascicle 31:
A Discourse by Fuhui.
Regarding the phrase "based on the nature of conditions (*pratyayatva*)," this means that because the preceding [condition] serves as the cause, it is subsequently termed the "nature of conditions."
Regarding the phrase "arising through conditions and giving rise to resolute conviction":

this means being able to understand that all internal and external phenomena produced by conditions possess only the nature of causes and the nature of conditions, and are devoid of a self, a person, or the like. Regarding the phrase "as explained at length elsewhere": [it refers to the detailed exposition found in other sources].
This refers to the fact that ignorance consists of nineteen types,
while formative forces (*saṃskāra*) consist of three types,
and so forth, as was extensively analyzed previously in the section on the "Investigation of the Arising of Defilements in the Grounds. As for the phrase "because of lack of mastery":
The term "self" (ātman) carries the meaning of sovereignty.
Because there is no sovereign self within ignorance, one does not form the thought:
"I am able to produce volitional formations."
All other cases should be understood accordingly. As for the phrase "in between," etc., this clarifies the meaning of emptiness (*śūnyatā*);

that is, because there is no dharma transmitted from one to another in the interval between the two dharmas of ignorance (*avidyā*) and volitional formations (*saṃskāra*), it is called empty. As for the phrase "as explained extensively before," [it refers to the preceding detailed exposition].

It is taught that [disputes] have harmful faults and disadvantages pertaining to both the present and future lives, as previously explained in the context of the meditation on impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*).
Regarding the phrase "all karmas," this refers to the three types of karma, such as wholesome (*kuśala*) and so forth. Regarding the phrase "the fruit of a single self-nature," it refers to...

This means that the dependent origination of both sentient and non-sentient things is comprehensively included. As for the phrase "the fruit of the enjoyment of objects," this refers exclusively to sentient beings.
As for the phrase "in this life and so forth," [it refers to the temporal dimension].
This refers to the arising of the resultant body within the five destinies in the present life.

"The six sense bases" refers to the six faculties. "Causing the sprout of existence to arise" means that with ignorance as the cause, the sprouts of the three types of volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) and so forth are produced.
This refutes the [view of] mutual dependence and so forth.

"The various graspings" refers to the grasping at self-theory (*ātma-vāda-parigraha*), the grasping at desire (*kāma-parigraha*), the grasping at precepts and observances (*śīla-vrata-parigraha*), and so on. "That which is internally realized" means...

This means that practitioners of the five stages directly perceive the two types of dharmas—those in direct and reverse order—such as ignorance and so forth, and are thus able to practice and realize the higher fruits. As for what is called "inferential dharma":
This means that by observing how various noble ones (ārya) cultivated the dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) in both forward and reverse order, they attained those noble fruits;
I too shall observe this practice and realize the higher fruit. Regarding the phrase "is able to correctly understand," etc.:
This refers to the fact that the six elements, such as earth and so forth, have distinct lineages (*gotra*) and are capable of conceptualization (*vitarka*). Regarding the meaning of "seed" (*bīja*):

it means that because the six factors, such as earth and so forth, serve as seeds, there are the bodies of the five destinies (*pañcagati*). Regarding the meaning of "cause" (*hetu*): [it refers to their status as the causal basis].
This means that because the six factors, such as the earth element and so forth, serve as causes, the bodies of the five destinies arise.

Regarding the meaning of "nature" (*dhātu*), it refers to the fact that each of these elements possesses its own specific nature, such as solidity and so forth. Regarding the meaning of "element" (*dhātu*), it refers to this very same sense.
Regarding the first of the four superior meanings: that which is called a "unified whole" (*ekapiṇḍasaṃjñā*) refers to failing to understand that within the body there are six elements (*ṣaḍdhātu*);
thus, to give rise merely to the view of a single self (*ātman*) is termed a "unified whole. Regarding the phrase "possessing correct reflection" (*samyagvitarka*), etc.:
This means that while various non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) maintain that it is because of a self (*ātman*) as the cause that one enters the mother’s womb, this is not the case here;
rather, it is because of the six elements (*ṣaḍdhātu*) that one enters the mother’s womb. As for the phrase "abiding in the nature of phenomena" (*dharmatā*):
This means that because the six elements—earth, water, and so forth—and all phenomena remain present whether Buddhas appear in the world or not, they are said to be "abiding.
Regarding the phrase "long inhalation," it refers to counting ten breaths as one unit, and so on. Regarding the phrase "entirely without holding the inhalation," and so forth:

This means that within the various conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) such as the aggregates (*skandha*), there is absolutely nothing that can maintain the two views of self and person (*ātman-pudgala*).
As for "cause," it refers to karma and afflictions (*kleśa*). As for "condition," it refers to...
This refers to the semen and blood of the parents and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "all practices," this refers to the characteristics of the fruit. Regarding the phrase "skillful means" and so forth, there is a question here.
Among the four types of objects of focus, the six meanings pertaining to the object of focus for pure conduct are as explained above;
their meaning is already known.
Third is the object of focus for skillfulness.
Regarding the fourth [type of object], the object for purifying afflictions (*kleśaviśodhana-ālambana*): why are the distinctions of its six aspects not mentioned?
Therefore, the treatise answers: "If one relies upon skillfulness (*kauśalya*) and so forth. As for the phrase "in this context":
This refers to the aforementioned four types of wisdom practicing contemplation through three gates and six matters regarding the impure;
the five contemplations are thus subsumed, for these nine kinds of preparatory practices ultimately perfect the previously mentioned contemplative gates.
Therefore, the treatise states "nine kinds" and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "attaining meditative concentration," it means that practitioners at the five stages, by means of the nine types of preparatory application (*prayoga*), swiftly attain the fundamental concentrations (*mauladhyāna*) of those five stages. Regarding the phrase "the stage to which one should proceed," and so forth:
This refers to the fact that practitioners in the five stages cultivate nine kinds of preparatory applications (*prayoga*).

For those in the initial stage of accumulation (*sambhāra-avasthā*), it means they will swiftly attain the stage of preparation (*prayoga-avasthā*) and so forth. As for the term "equal parts" (*sama-bhāga*):
This means that because the five categories of afflictions, such as greed and so forth, do not reside exclusively in one [category], they are called "equally distributed" (*sabhāga*).

As for the term "those with thin dust" (*tanu-rajas*), it refers to those who are practitioners of the higher stages among the five categories. Regarding the phrase "should follow according to what is desired," etc.:

This refers to the fact that among the five categories of afflictions, [the treatise] first addresses which ones arise for the two types of practitioners, such as the "Equal-Practice" (Samacarita) and others, by means of the gateway of cultivating their antidotes.
Therefore, the text of the treatise cites "having a single object of focus" (*ekālambanatā*) and so forth. As for the phrase "associated, object-conditioned," and so on:
This refers to the five contemplative gateways, such as the meditation on impurity and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "not fully entering," the term "conforming" and so on refers to the mind during the three periods of beginning, middle, and end. Regarding the phrase "by abiding in such [a state]," etc.:
This means that abiding prior to [the fruit], and so forth, the three types of application—such as the six dharmas like "emergence" (*vyutthāna*)—being non-lax is called "heedfulness" (*apramāda*).
Regarding the phrases "one period" (*ekakāla*) and "half a period" (*ardhakāla*), they refer to one watch (*yāma*) or half a watch. Regarding the "dharma and its meaning" (*dharmārtha*):
This means that within the meaning of the phenomena of the "remedied" (*pratipakṣa*) and the "remedy" (*pratipakṣika*), there is no inversion.

Regarding the phrase "the ninefold aspects of mental abiding," this refers to the nine ways of settling the mind, beginning with internal abiding (*adhyātma-sthāpanā*). Regarding the term "signless" (*animitta*):
This refers to the mind that is free from the notions of "self" and "what belongs to self.

Regarding the statement "all attain purity," it means that by relying on the stage of analytical contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) to break through [delusions], both [the subject and object] are accomplished in mutual purity; thus it is said "all," and so forth. Regarding the statement "all preparatory practices" (*prayoga*):
This refers to the preparatory application (*prayoga*) of the categories of calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*). Regarding the phrase "that which is perfumed" (*bhāvita*) and so forth:
it means that insight is regarded as the perfumer (*bhāvaka*), while calm abiding is regarded as the object to be perfumed (*bhāvya*).
Because these two dharmas depend upon one another, both attain purification. Regarding the statement "all preparatory practices" (*prayoga*):

this refers to the category of insight (*vipaśyanā*), because it serves as the preparatory practice for the category of calm abiding (*śamatha*). Regarding the phrase "by means of which," etc.: [it refers to the fact that] by means of these, [the path is accomplished].
This means that among the six recollections (*ṣaḍ-anusmṛti*) and so forth, taking up any one of them is termed "exertion" (*pragraha*). Regarding the phrase "manifesting" (*saṃdarśana*) and so forth:

it means that when the mind is sunken, one manifests the mind by means of pure and sublime signs, encouraging the mind and congratulating the mind. Regarding the phrase "conforming" (*anuloma*) and so forth: [it refers to...]

This means that among the five contemplations, such as that of the impure and so forth, being diligent and energetic is the characteristic of "arousing" (pragraha). Regarding the phrase "the object of focus" and so on:
it means that within the mind, there is no defilement toward objects that are either agreeable or disagreeable, because the mind is equanimous.

It also functions with equality within śamatha and vipaśyanā. Regarding the statement "by means of the object of focus," this means that when the mind does not dwell upon either the favorable or the unfavorable, nor upon śamatha or vipaśyanā, it is called the characteristic of equanimity (*upekṣā*). As for the term "higher equanimity":
This refers to the relinquishment of higher and higher stages.

Regarding the phrase "referring to such as these," it means that one attains skillfulness in each and every aspect of the objects of the two dharmas of śamatha and vipaśyanā, as described above. Regarding the phrase "skillfully grasping" and so forth:
This refers to the three moments of mind at the beginning, middle, and end.
As for the phrase "sometimes relinquishing," it means that if one relinquishes the images associated with mundane or supramundane meditative concentration, it is called "emerging from concentration."
If one engages in mental attention regarding matters such as seeking alms while in an indeterminate state, this is not yet called "emerging from meditative absorption.
Regarding the phrase "in other activities," it refers to the pursuit of the higher and higher fruits within the practice. Regarding the phrase "in all [activities]," etc.:
This means that among the trainings of the precepts one has received, being without transgression is called "not abandoning the yoke.
This means that practicing within the eight factors such as being without holes or breaches is called "not transgressing. As for the phrase "regarding what has been practiced for a long time," etc.:
This means that regarding one's own performed actions of body, speech, and mind,
one refrains from all unwholesome deeds and practices in accordance with the ten wholesome courses of action.
Therefore, the treatise states that it is "due to the recollection of the causes" and so forth. Regarding the phrase "repeatedly generating resolute conviction," this refers to the path of antidotes.
Regarding the phrase "repeatedly and correctly dispelling," [it refers to the abandonment of the objects of negation].
This refers to the dharmas that are to be remedied.
The Sanskrit term *vighāta* fully encompasses both of the aforementioned meanings.
First, the meaning of resolute conviction (*adhimukti*);
second, the meaning of elimination (*vibhāvanā*).

Since these two are both correct preparatory practices (*samyak-prayoga*), these two names are designated. Regarding the phrase "practicing according to the characteristics" (*lakṣaṇānupraviṣṭa*) and so forth:
This means that within each of the twenty virtuous meditative concentrations, there is a corresponding antidote for the objects to be remedied and the removal of those very objects;
this should also be understood to apply to the beginner practitioner herein.
One who has long cultivated the practice of contemplation and fully cultivates both of the aforementioned two practices is called a "right practitioner.
Regarding the phrase "one should know that among these," each of these five gates possesses both the meaning of cause and the meaning of fruit.
The speaker should understand that the phrase "due to the initial [state], etc.

means that those who practice the contemplation of impurity (*aśubhabhāvanā*) and so forth necessarily turn their backs on the inverted characteristics of tranquility (*śamatha*) and the like. The phrase "due to taking other concentrations as objects," etc., [should be understood accordingly].

This means that if the power of the meditative concentration (*samādhi*) cultivated on the path is weak and thus cannot eliminate the factors to be abandoned (*vipakṣa*), one should cultivate other concentrations to act as its auxiliaries so as to perfect the primary concentration. Regarding the phrase "due to all," etc.:

This means that for one who gives rise to defilement regarding such signs as the pure and so forth, one should cultivate the contemplation of the impure and so forth to eliminate those signs such as the pure. As for the phrase "though established as universal," etc.:
In this regard, a question is raised:
regarding the five types of characteristics described in the sūtras as "to be eliminated" (*vibhāvanā*), what is the intended meaning of "correct elimination"?
Therefore, the treatise answers:
However, within this context, there are five difficulties regarding the term "equality" (*madhya*).
Here, only the first two methods are taken to establish the process of elimination (*vibhāvanā*). As for the statement: "One does not at all bind the mind to the object of focus (*ālambana*)."
This means that because the faculties and dispositions of practitioners vary and their afflictions differ,
when first beginning their practice, those with a predominance of sensual desire are directed to bind their minds through the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*).
If one has an abundance of anger, one should bind the mind by means of the contemplation of loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
The rest should be understood accordingly;
thus, the treatise states, "or again, dwelling [upon them]," and so forth. Regarding the phrase, "one should simply form this thought," and so on:
That is to say, when within the signs of the contemplation of impurity and so forth there are signs of purity and so forth, it is called "distraction";
when there are signs of impurity and so forth, it is called "non-distraction.
A beginner should form this thought:
"How shall my mind be free from distraction?
This means: "At what time shall I attain association with non-distraction regarding dharmas such as impurity (*aśubhā*)?
The following nine types are each explained in conjunction with the phrase "merely thinking thus" (*iti manasikāra*). Regarding the term "lack of tranquility" (*apraśānta*):
"Because one abandons active manifestation" refers to the cessation of the seeds and their active manifestation;
"fierce tranquility" refers to the abandonment of both the seeds and active manifestation. The phrase "thus with diligent effort, etc.
corresponds individually to each of the ten preceding points. The phrase "precisely by means of such [effort], etc. [refers to the aforementioned].

This means that because one takes internal withdrawal of the mind as the cause, practitioners at the five stages do not attend to mental orientations such as "purity" regarding objects of observation such as the impure. Regarding the term "with signs" (*sanimitta*):

This refers to the aspect of impurity and so forth. To say "possessing conceptual differentiation" means that there is a conceptually differentiated image, such as that of impurity and so forth. To say "by way of conforming to the aspects and so forth" means...
This refers to practicing the three types of wisdom, such as investigation (*vitarka*) and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "their objects," it means that by relying on these three types of wisdom, one is able to contemplate the five contemplations of impurity and so forth, as well as their defects and virtues.
It is not that one practices only the single contemplation of impurity;
therefore, the treatise states "not exclusively" (*naikāntika*) and so forth. Regarding the phrase "furthermore, relinquishing," etc., there is a question herein.
When practicing the five contemplations, are they to be employed solely with the three types of wisdom as the means (*upāya*), or should other dharmas also be used as the means?
Therefore, the treatise answers that it is "by means of the characteristics of returning," etc. Regarding the phrase "due to the object of focus" (*ālambana*), etc.:
This means that if one abandons *śamatha*, one will necessarily become distracted; therefore, it is called "equanimity" (*upekṣā*).
Because it is subsumed under the category of *śamatha* through the nine modes of mental abiding, it is called "non-abandonment. As for the phrase "right upon the object of focus," etc.:
This means that by means of observing through the sixfold distinctions such as the meaning (*artha*) and so forth,
one does not form the conceptual signs (*nimitta*) regarding the objects to be countered, does not conceive of them as "I," and does not give rise to the discriminating mind of "I" and "mine."

Therefore, it is called "non-appropriation. Regarding the phrase "there being [the practice] therein," this means that by means of the nine ways of abiding the mind as the cause, one is able to dwell securely in contemplations such as the foul.
Regarding the phrase "because of taking up the practice of cessation," etc.:
This means that by investigating the distinctions among the six objects, such as the meaning (*artha*) and so forth, one seeks after impurity and the like;
thus, it serves as the skillful means for the category of *śamatha*.
Therefore, it is called "the aspect of the object of knowledge that is the objective support for the practice of *śamatha*. As for the phrase "if, with respect to the object," and so forth:
That is to say, resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*) is insight (*vipaśyanā*),

while elimination is calm abiding (*śamatha*). Regarding the phrase "by means of repeated resolute conviction" and the phrase "toward a narrow object," this refers to the time when one practices the five contemplations,
such as the meditation on impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*).
First, one contemplates the finger joints as being narrow and small;
this gradual increase is called "vastness.
Finally, one contemplates the ten directions as being immeasurable.

Therefore, the treatise states "vastness" and so forth. Regarding the phrase "if all dharmas," this refers to the twenty virtuous meditative absorptions (*śubha-vimokṣa*), such as the bloated corpse (*vinīlaka*) and others;
these are all material images (*rūpa-pratibimba*). Regarding the phrase "all formless dharmas,"...

This means that all images produced by the four contemplations, such as loving-kindness and compassion, are merely manifestations of mental phenomena; therefore, they are called "non-material" (*arūpa*).
"Renunciation" refers to the fruit of *nirvāṇa*. "Detachment" refers to...
This refers to the cause of nirvāṇa. "Defiled longing" means being attached to the five desires and lacking the mind of renunciation. "Not delighting," and so forth, refers to...
This means that within the dharmas of the causes and effects of nirvāṇa, there is no mind of joyful aspiration, but rather the arising of distress and affliction.
Regarding "inferior wisdom and vision," this refers to giving rise to arrogance when one realizes only a small portion during the path of uninterrupted liberation (*ānantarya-mārga*).

Therefore, the text of the treatise says, "thinking 'I can attain,' and so forth. Regarding the statement "as explained at length previously," it means that [the thought] "only I can attain," and so forth, has already been explained at length in the previous section on the Stage of Renunciation (*nairyāṇika-bhūmi*).
Regarding the statement "referring to those things conducive to the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), etc.," it refers to those factors that accord with the hindrances.
That is to say, among the factors that accord with the bases for the five hindrances,
improper attention (*ayoniśomanasikāra*) is termed an obstruction;
the self-exaltation resulting from discursive thought (*vitarka*) is to be understood according to what was previously explained.
These three all arise from improper mental attention (*ayoniśo-manasikāra*), and are therefore called "causal conditions" (*hetu-pratyaya*).
"Causal condition" is the fundamental meaning [of this term]. As for the phrase "thoroughly knowing," etc.:
This means that due to the four obstacles such as cowardice and so forth, four kinds of faults arise. Regarding the phrase "the four kinds [of faults]":
first is the fault of not attaining what has not yet been attained.
This refers to the fact that one has not yet realized, nor does one realize, both the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).
Second is the fault of losing knowledge through regression;
third is the fault of destroying the preparatory application (*prayoga*).

Regarding the four afflictions and the five faults of the dharmas such as those with outflows: the phrase "generally employing recollection and so forth" refers to the six recollections (*ṣaḍ-anusmṛti*).
The phrase "employing diligence and so forth" [refers to the remaining factors].
This means that through application, one remedies weakness;
through equanimity, one remedies excessive physical exertion;
and through thorough penetration, one remedies the fault of initial practice. Regarding the phrase "by means of those opposites," etc.:

This means that because one counteracts the five factors—namely, the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), discursive thought (*vitarka*), self-exaltation (*auddhatya*), and the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-saṃjñā*)—it is said, "Furthermore, thoroughly understanding," and so forth.
If one does not understand that these various hindrances possess the nature of being hindrances, [one cannot overcome them].
Because one is unable to cultivate the remedies,

the first [point] establishes the essential nature of thorough knowledge (*parijñā*). Regarding the phrase "distancing from causes and conditions," it means that if one does not know the causes and conditions for the arising of various hindrances.
One will certainly not know the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Regarding the statement "to be far removed from causes and conditions":

this means that if one does not know the causes and conditions for the arising of various obstacles, one will certainly be unable to cultivate the practice of the remedies (*pratipakṣa*). Regarding the statement "to accord with the teaching": [it refers to...]
This means that because the phenomena to be countered (*vipakṣa*) observed in accordance [with the path] are of many kinds, the teachings that counteract them are likewise of many kinds.

Thus, regarding the phrase "Vipaśyanā and so forth," it is called "many" because within each individual observation (*vipaśyanā*), a corresponding instance of calm abiding (*śamatha*) arises. As for the phrase "the objects of knowledge" (*jñeya-viṣaya*):

This refers to the meaning of cause and effect within the categories of defilement and purity as observed through the three gates and six matters. Regarding the phrase "physical pliancy and so forth," there is a question here:
at what time do practitioners of the five stages bring these two dharmas to perfection?
Therefore, the treatise answers: "If one attains the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), etc.
If an Arhat transforms the basis of the defiled category into the pure category, only then does one attain the ultimate. Regarding the phrase "the objects of knowledge" (*jñeya-vastu*):

This refers to that which is to be remedied and the path that remedies it. Regarding the phrase "that which accords with sensual desire and so forth," it means that among the remedial factors— such as the beauty of a woman—
the initial mind does not yet enter into them.
The mind does not find delight in the center,
nor does the subsequent mind have faith or understanding. Regarding the phrase "and so forth,
as extensively explained," this refers to objects that accord with anger and are disagreeable conditions.
At first they do not enter;
in the middle they do not find delight;
and in the end they lack faith and understanding.
Up to this point, it is called the contemplation of loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
Whether it has reached its ultimate consummation or not is as explained previously regarding the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*).
The three lower contemplations are all explained according to this principle.

Regarding the phrase "conforming to the dharmas of ignorance," this means that within the dharmas of dependent origination throughout the three periods of time, giving rise to the four inversions of permanence, bliss, self, and purity conforms to the production of the dharmas of ignorance. Regarding the phrase "not the characteristic of an aggregate of the body," [it refers to the absence of such a self].
This means that one does not give rise to the notion of a single aggregate as a self from within the body.

Regarding "conceptual proliferation" (*prapañca*), it refers to manifold discrimination, such as thoughts of sensual desire and so forth. Regarding the phrase "in the contemplation of phenomena" (*dharmānupaśyanā*) and so on:

This means that by relying upon meditative concentration (*samādhi*), the predominant wisdom (*adhiprajñā*) operates within the contemplation of the object of focus, wherein the object to be countered and its antidote are perceived. As for the term "universal characteristic" (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*):
This refers to the objects of observation for the five contemplations, such as the impure and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "by means of this mental attention," it means that it is caused by the five types of mental attention, such as the impure and so forth.
It causes the mind to feel weary of and detached from the five kinds of loathsome phenomena, such as purity, permanence, and bliss.
The [explanations for] the three subsequent modes of attention (*manasikāra*) should all be understood according to this principle. As for the phrase "regarding phenomena that are to be cherished":
This means that because [contemplations] such as the impure are the supreme dharmas;

the phrase "by these conditions" means by taking the five contemplations, such as the impure, as causes, one is able to abandon all seeds of the perception of purity within body and mind. The phrase "inner mental tranquility" refers to this.
This refers to the five contemplations, such as that on impurity and so forth.

What is called "contemplation of phenomena" (dharmānupaśyanā) refers to the characteristics of the increase and decrease of the objects to be remedied and their remedies within these five contemplations. As for what is called "outflows" (āsrava):
This refers to the various inverted perceptions, such as [perceiving] purity and so forth.

What are called "objects of the outflows" (āsravasthānīyā dharmāḥ) refer to objects that are agreeable or disagreeable, such as men, women, and the like. What is called "the arising of fever" (paridāha) refers to...
This refers to the arising of revulsion and detachment toward a limited portion of the objects of feverish affliction and outflows (*āsrava*).
As for the term "equally feverish," it refers to the arising of the aspect of revulsion and detachment toward all objects of feverish affliction and outflows without exception.
Regarding the two phrases beginning with "giving rise to revulsion below," they are explained according to this principle:

as for the statement "referring to one's own decline and loss," it means that if a practitioner at any of the five stages suffers the loss of personal wealth and profit, or encounters physical decline and calamities such as illness and so forth, [they should give rise to revulsion].
This is called one's own decline;
others are likewise the same.
These two objects are the points of aversion for a practitioner.
Therefore, the treatise states, "because of frequent reflection," and so forth.
This means that by reflecting upon phenomena characterized by decay and loss, one is able to afflict oneself and others. Regarding the phrase, "if one prospers for oneself," and so forth:

Although there may be prosperous events for oneself and others, they ultimately all fall into the nature of decay, the nature of exhaustion, the nature of destruction, the nature of dissolution, and the nature of transformation; therefore, one should give rise to weary detachment. As for the term "ford" (*tīrtha*):
This refers to the initial association with meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
"Expansion" means that the concentration gradually moistens the subsequent moments of mind.
"Fusion and adaptation" refers to the later stage. "Realization of purity" refers to...
This refers to the lightness and ease (*praśrabdhi*) of body and mind.
As for the phrase "thinking thus," etc., this sentence corresponds respectively with each of the two [remaining] jewels below. As for the phrase "if my merit now," etc.:

This means that because one has the virtue of ethical discipline (*śīla*) as a companion, one will go to a happy destination (*sugati*) when life ends or one passes away. Regarding the phrase "practicing the holy life together" (*sabrahmacārin*), this indicates the six forms of harmonious respect (*ṣaḍvidha-sāmīcī*) in accordance with the Dharma.
Regarding the phrase "due to [the order of] before and after," etc., it refers to the sequence of events.
This refers to practitioners at the five stages who reflect as follows:
"Because I have previously applied diligent effort and subsequently cultivated [the path] within the five types of contemplation, such as that on impurity."
One will certainly obtain the fruit of the five contemplations;

thus, the treatise states, "by means of recollecting the dharmas," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "that which is conducive," it refers to taking the cultivation of mental attention (*manasikāra*) as the cause.
For one who practices contemplations such as that on impurity,
among the outflowing phenomena of purity and so forth,
they do not initially direct their inclination toward them.
Second, they are able to oppose; third, they are able to bring about joy;

and fourth, they are able to cause separation, because each abides in its own fundamental meditative concentration (*mauladhyāna*). Regarding the phrase "toward things that are to be rejoiced in," etc.:
This means that by means of the five contemplations conducive to joy, such as the contemplation of impurity, the mind is gladdened and moistened;
thus, one is initially able to emerge from the inverted perceptions of purity and so forth.
Second, it causes the mind to take up its direction;
third, it uplifts the faculties;
fourth, it brings about joyful concord.

These four serve as the respective antidotes to the four aforementioned factors, such as non-directionality and so forth. Regarding the phrase "from time to time" and so on, it means that they arise by taking the production of pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) as their cause.
It is capable of generating the four types of wisdom-practice that resolve all phenomena, such as those pertaining to defilement and purity.
Regarding the phrase "using them as tools for work," this refers to using items such as a furnace, bellows, tongs, and a hammer. Regarding the phrase "thus encouraging practice" and so forth:
This corresponds point by point with what follows below. Regarding the phrase "each and every" and so forth:

it means that within each of the meditative gateways such as the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) being practiced, each one is joined with the simultaneous application of both calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*).
First, one is able to attend closely to the administration;
second, one is able to bring about skillful harmony;
third, by relying on meditative concentration, one does not waver, meaning that the mind does not regress.
Fourth, regarding the absence of movement within meditative concentration (*samādhi*), and so forth.
The hand-notes for the thirty-first fascicle of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* are complete.
Hand-notes for the thirty-second fascicle of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.
Regarding the discourse on "establishing merit and wisdom according to what is heard":
the intent here is to ask about the person who first practices the five contemplations, such as the meditation on impurity.
For one who wishes to cultivate mental attention (*manasikāra*) toward the impure and so forth,
by what means should that spiritual friend cause them to abide in the five kinds of signs, such as revulsion (*nirveda*)?
Therefore, the treatise states, "as they should be established," and so forth. Regarding the mention of "hearing" and so on:

although this section relies upon the gate of the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) for the purpose of generating revulsion, the same question applies equally to those who practice the contemplation of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and other such meditations. As for the phrase "the fire of the household":
This refers to sons, daughters, and others who do not carry on the family lineage.

As for the phrase "if you see before your eyes," etc., it means that if one sees others—oneself, one's own kin, and even entire villages—undergoing suffering, one should give rise to a sense of weary detachment (*nirveda*).
The speaker should know that the detailed explanation is as previously stated:
namely, one should cultivate a sense of weary detachment toward those who encounter suffering and hardship within one's own person, one's own retinue, and one's own village or town.
As previously stated: "cultivation" refers to the manifestation of illness;
"the dharma-nature of illness" refers to the seeds and habitual tendencies of illness.

Death is also to be understood according to this. Regarding the phrase "by reason of these causes and conditions" and so forth, it means that suffering and affliction arise due to three kinds of characteristics pertaining to others' bodies, retinues, villages, towns, and so on. Regarding the phrase "precisely by means of these matters," [it refers to the aforementioned objects].
It is because, through the arising of weariness toward matters such as prosperity and decline, one is able to reach the end of suffering.

Regarding the phrase "in the abandonment," it means that one is able to abandon the five factors—purity and so forth—that are to be abandoned by the five contemplations. Regarding the phrase "I may lose mindfulness" and so on:

This means that the following four phrases clarify the meaning of observation according to their specific characteristics. The phrase "regarding all training, there are contradictions and explanations, etc.
corresponds to each of the aforementioned four phrases one by one. As for the term "original nature" (prakṛti):
This refers to the mind seeking precepts at the time of receiving them. Regarding the phrase "to state it briefly," etc., there is a question here:
what does the meaning of these two types of observation—general and specific—reveal?
Therefore, the treatise answers by saying, "Regarding all the points of training (*śikṣāpada*) and so forth.
This means that two types of examination are established because both the present points of training and the preparatory application (*prayoga*) are perfected. As for the term *śīlabhū*:
This means that if one has committed a transgression against the śīla, one will necessarily subsequently give rise to regret.

Regarding the phrase "furthermore, removing obstacles and so forth," it means that by virtue of joy, one is able to remove all obstacles. Regarding the phrase "such as the characteristics of practice and so forth," [it refers to...]
In this regard, a question is asked:
regarding the three terms— joy (*prīti*), gladness (*saumanasya*), and mental satisfaction (*saumanasya*)— as they are taught in the various holy scriptures, what is the distinction between them?
Therefore, the treatise answers by stating "first, name and so forth. As for the phrase "you, regarding abandonment, reduction,
and so on," it means that by means of training, refining, and moistening the mind,
one is able to abandon worldly greed and sorrow.

And as for the statement "if it is thus," etc., it means that because of the characteristic of wearying detachment, one turns away from all dark qualities (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*); and because of the characteristic of joyful aspiration, one turns toward all white qualities (*śuklapakṣa*). Furthermore, regarding the attainment of the two supramundane dharmas of calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*): because of the characteristic of wearying detachment, one turns away from all dark qualities;
and because of the characteristic of joyful aspiration, one turns toward all white qualities.
Therefore, the text of the treatise states, "by means of training the mind and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "the various characteristics and so forth," this refers to the ten characteristics consisting of the objects such as form (*rūpa*), as well as birth, aging, sickness, and male and female. Regarding the phrase "the eight beginning with desire":
This refers to desire, ill-will, harmfulness, the void, the realm, kinsmen, and immortality;

it also refers to the objects previously experienced. Regarding the phrase "desire, greed, and so forth," this means that the five factors to be remedied by the five contemplations—such as the contemplation of impurity—are called secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*).

"It is not the five hindrances. Regarding the statement "therefore, such as these," it means that each of the three factors—such as the [three] characteristics (lakṣaṇa)—possesses five kinds of faults, namely: being suffering, non-noble, and so forth. Regarding the statement "furthermore, one should [regard] etc.," it means...
That is to say, by means of the three types of mind— such as one-pointedness of mind and so forth—
one is able to give rise to six modes of activity,
each serving as an antidote to the three preceding faults.
These six kinds of dharmas are all free from the establishment of views such as the self (*ātman*) posited by non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
Regarding the phrase "or lamp-light, etc.," it means that if, while practicing [meditations] such as the foul (*aśubha*), the aforementioned faults arise.
One should gradually cultivate the four kinds of samādhis, such as the fire-light samādhi and others.

Regarding the phrase "having already grasped these," it means that although one who cultivates the contemplation of impurity (aśubha-bhāvanā) is able to grasp the sign of light while remaining in the contemplation of impurity.

Because one must further discern the twenty types [of corpses], such as the bluish-livid corpse (*vinīlaka*), when the power of habitual practice causes the aspect of purity to appear, it is said: "First, with respect to a single object," and so forth.
This means that among the five contemplations, such as that of impurity and so forth,
one is able to bind the mind to any one object and turn away from the five kinds of perversions, such as the perception of purity and so forth. Regarding the phrase "furthermore, within these," etc.:
This means that for one who is able to understand these six aspects, distraction and non-distraction naturally manifest before them.
Regarding the phrase "right within those," it means that when distortions such as [the notion of] purity arise, one does not follow after those thoughts. Regarding the term "all virtues":
This refers to those who are the most handsome among the multitude, such as men and women.
As for the phrase "these very various virtues," this analogy is derived from the *Āgama Sūtras* and the *Satyaka-irreṇya-putra Sūtra*.
The World-Honored One was staying in the kingdom of Ujjenī.
King Pālita, having invited the Buddha and provided him with various musical performances, addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"Regarding the music I have now provided, is there anything else superior to this music?"
The World-Honored One said:
"I have heard nothing at all.
Who can judge the quality of the music you perform?"
The king said,
"I have personally seen and heard the music performed above;
why do you not distinguish it?"

The World-Honored One established this analogy based on its underlying principle. Regarding the phrase "the great and so forth arise," "and so forth" refers to the gathering of various kinds of people.
Regarding the phrase "by means of this, it can cause [them] to be equal," it means...

This means that because the authentic teaching serves as the cause, six kinds of beneficial fruits—such as the continuity of a mind free from attachment—arise within the five stages of contemplation. As for the term "right mindfulness":
The "Chapter on Cessation" (Śamatha-varga) speaks of that which is practiced together with right knowledge;
this refers to the "Chapter on Insight" (Vipaśyanā-varga). The intention here is to clarify this point.

For one who practices the five contemplations, within each individual contemplation, it is essential that stillness (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*) be practiced in tandem (*yuganaddha*) for it to be called "skillful cultivation. What is termed "non-conceptual" belongs to the category of stillness; what is termed "conceptual" [belongs to the category of insight].
This refers to the "Chapter on Contemplation" (*vipaśyanā-varga*). Regarding the phrase "at the time of entering," etc.,

the intended meaning here is that the previously mentioned signs of the bloated corpse (*vinīlaka*) and so forth are designated as "provisional" (*prajñapti*) because they arise from a gradual accumulation [of parts].

Now, this true characteristic should be contemplated as follows: all the livid-blue corpses of oneself and others from beginningless time are beyond calculation; therefore, it is called "the real. As for the phrase "and not through cultivation," etc.:
This means that one does not achieve mastery through meditative observation merely by repeatedly practicing the visualization of the livid corpse and so forth;
rather, it is called "long-term uniformity" because at all times, one is able to spontaneously perceive signs such as impurity without relying on deliberate effort.
This is called the characteristic of the completion of contemplation;

thus, the treatise says, "for that duration of time," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "the various characteristics do not appear," it means that within this stage, all characteristics such as purity and so on no longer manifest. Regarding the phrase "not causing [them] to be abandoned,"...
Furthermore, because one does not abandon the category of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), it is called "signless" (*animitta*);
this means the absence of the ten signs, such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth. It is called "non-conceptual" (*avikalpa*);
this means the absence of the eight kinds of discursive thought (*vitarka*). It is called "tranquil" (*śānta*).
This means that there are no five secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*). Regarding the "mind accompanied by radiance," this refers to the light of a lamp.
Regarding the "mind accompanied by illumination," this refers to the light of fire.
Regarding the "mind accompanied by clarity and purity," [this refers to...]
The "light of the sun" refers to the radiance of the sun. The "light of non-darkness" refers to the radiance of the moon.
The phrase "cultivating śamatha and so forth" is to be understood as corresponding one-to-one with each of the four preceding texts. The term "narrow and small" means:
This means that observing a single person and so forth is termed "narrow and small.
Regarding the phrase "repeatedly" and so on, it corresponds one-to-one with each of the four preceding textual passages. Regarding the phrase "toward those whom one loves" and so on:

This means that regarding one's own beloved body, one should recognize that it must inevitably die and be carried to the cemetery, where the twenty signs, such as the bluish discoloration (*vinīlaka*), gradually arise. As for the phrase "repeatedly," etc.:
Each of these is combined with the aforementioned [contemplations] such as the bluish-black discoloration (*vinīlaka*).

Regarding the statement, "Furthermore, you should [contemplate] the aggregates," this means that because the four formless aggregates (*arūpaskandha*) are all suffering, impermanent, and non-self, they are termed the contemplation of the three dharmas, beginning with feeling (*vedanā*). Regarding the term "signless" (*animitta*):
This refers to the ten aspects, such as formlessness, which are observed by relying on the categories of feeling, mind, and phenomena.
"Non-conceptual" means that it is free from the eight kinds of discursive thought. "Quiescent" means...
Because it is devoid of the five secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*):
"devoid of activity" means there is no agent-self (*kartṛ-ātman*);
"devoid of longing" means there is no conceptual proliferation (*vitarka*) regarding faults; "devoid of agitation" means...
This means that because form and so forth are not subject to agitation;
"free from burning affliction" means being without defilements; "the bliss of quiescence" means realizing nirvāṇa;
and "acting upon the objects of perception and so forth" refers to the following.

This means that because the objects of form (*rūpa*) and so forth do not cause disturbance; as for the phrase "the four formless aggregates (*arūpaskandha*) and so forth," it refers to the fact that feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) undergo moment-to-moment transformation; and as for the phrase "you should [apply this] to these," it refers to those very things.
This corresponds point by point with the ten preceding passages. Regarding the term "undisturbed" (*amukhara*):
according to the Tibetan version, it does not say "undisturbed" but rather "distracted" (*vikṣipta*).
The intended meaning here is as follows:

Because one observes that distraction arises from the three phenomena of feeling and so forth, one is then able to cultivate the contemplation of impermanence and other characteristics regarding those three phenomena; this is called "non-distraction. As for the words "you all," [it means]:
That which turns according to conditions upon the three objects, such as sensation (*vedanā*) and so forth, is called the "unstable stage" (*aniyata-bhūmi*).

Regarding the statement that "the past is exhausted and ceased," it is because sensation and the others are all phenomena that have already fallen away. Regarding the statement "loss of mindfulness" (*muṣitasmṛti*):
If one takes the three dharmas beginning with sensation as objects, one loses right mindfulness; therefore, it is said that they "arise from a distracted mind.
This is because all three dharmas arise from a distracted mind.
The three [dharmas] beginning with characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are explained according to the same principle as before. As for the term "predominant" (*adhipati*):
Because the three [feelings], such as sensation (*vedanā*), give rise to the three inversions (*viparyāsa*), such as pleasure (*sukha*), it is said, "You should [know]," and so forth;
this corresponds point by point with each of the preceding passages. Regarding the phrase, "these various phenomena (*dharma*) and so forth":
This means that the three dharmas, beginning with sensation (*vedanā*), are ultimately all characterized by the five aspects such as being produced by deception and illusion.
The phrase "you should" and so forth corresponds one-to-one with each of the five preceding statements. The phrase "you should [regard] this" and so forth [is explained as follows].
This refers to relinquishing the objects of focus, such as pleasure. Regarding "filthy seats and bedding," this refers to places where men and women engage in sexual intercourse.
Regarding "constant practice," this refers to the deeds performed by those in training (śaikṣa).
Regarding "ultimate practice," [it refers to the deeds of those beyond training].
These are the deeds of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).

Both of these involve two kinds of application (*prayoga*): that which is immediate and that which is grave. Regarding the phrase "attaining the inferior," it refers to attaining the fruits of one in training (*śaikṣa*).
Regarding the phrase "vast and perfect," it refers to [the attainment of the fruit of] one beyond training.
This refers to the stage of one beyond training (aśaikṣa).
"Bliss free from fault" refers to supramundane bliss.
"Sensual bliss" refers to the bliss of the desire realm (kāmadhātu). "Bliss accompanied by joy" refers to...
This refers to the bliss of the first dhyāna.
As for the phrase "bliss without joy," it refers to the bliss from the second dhyāna up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. Regarding the distinctions among these:
This refers to the specific characteristics of the four contemplations, such as loving-kindness (*maitrī*), which will be explained one by one below.
Regarding the phrase "at the time of entering," it means at the time of entering the contemplation of loving-kindness.
Regarding the phrase "the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) and so forth," [it refers to...]
This means that the three [faculties] beginning with feeling can destroy the three kinds of perversions such as pleasure; thus they are called "destructive conditions" (*bhaṅga-pratyaya*).
Regarding the term "manifest form" (*vijñapti-rūpa*), it refers to wholesome and unwholesome manifest matter. Regarding the term "only the mindfulness of the body" (*kāya-smṛtyupasthāna*):
This refers to establishing mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) upon the three types of persons—enemies, relatives, and neutral parties.

Regarding "the mental engagement of resolute conviction" (adhimokṣa-manasikāra), it refers to the mental engagement with provisional characteristics (parikalpita-lakṣaṇa). Regarding the phrase "Furthermore, I [regard] them... and so forth:

If one does not give rise to loving-kindness toward sentient beings who have passed away in the past, one will be unable to eradicate the seeds and habitual tendencies of anger within the *ālayavijñāna*. As for the phrase "immeasurable and exceedingly great," it means:

This means that within the past lives, one gives rise to a mind of loving-kindness and compassion toward all those who were enemies or kin, which surpasses the previous cultivation based on provisional signs; yet it is said to be "not truly real."

This means that what is not non-ultimate reality is indeed ultimate reality. The term *yāpanīyasatya-bhāga* is a Sanskrit expression; here it is translated as "the portion of the cause that is insufficient.
As for the statement "the details are as previously explained," [it refers to the preceding discourse].
That is to say, the categories of tranquility (śamatha), non-distraction (avikṣepa), and insight (vipaśyanā)—
the meaning of these three doors should be explained here,
as they are not distinct from the meaning of the contemplation of impurity (aśubhabhāvanā).
Therefore, this is not mentioned here. As for "discriminating and grasping at signs," it refers to a beginner who, by grasping at the four inversions, wanders through birth and death;
yet, by grasping at the sign of non-inversion, they attain liberation from birth and death. As for "producing the fundamental karma":
This refers to the causes of various karmas, such as wholesome and unwholesome actions.
As for the phrase "if regarding one's own body," it means contemplating one's own body as suffering, empty, impermanent, and so forth.
The following sections on the external body and the bodies of others are to be understood as identical to what has been explained here.

Regarding the statement "the rest is as previously explained," this refers to the *Āśraya-varga* (Chapter on the Basis), the *Avikṣepa-varga* (Chapter on Non-distraction), and the *Vipaśyanā-varga* (Chapter on Insight), which clarify the characteristics of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
As previously explained in the *Aśubhabhāvanā* (Contemplation of Impurity):
"The term 'arrayed days' refers to the period of extreme heat;
'blazing' refers to the seasonal miasma diseases; and 'spreading creepers' refers to..."
This means that the fire is never extinguished. Regarding the phrase "subtle discernment":
it means that while the first five elements are easily understood because they are coarse and manifest, the characteristics of this consciousness-element are subtle;
therefore, one must rely on the practitioner’s subtle discernment before its characteristics can be fully realized. Regarding the phrase "having realized these characteristics," etc.:

This means that one should understand that within the body composed of the four great elements, there is only the seed and the planted state of the aggregate of consciousness (vijñāna-skandha), which by its own nature is capable of cognizing objects and is devoid of self. As for the term "throat-tube":
This refers to the cavity of the throat and the distension of the stomach. Regarding the phrase "in ten kinds" and so forth,
it refers to the ten types of derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*).
Therefore, because it is the objective basis,
one analyzes the dependent consciousness from this [basis]. To say that it "far exceeds this" means that this true characteristic surpasses that conventional characteristic.
This means that they are immeasurable. Regarding the phrase "a single part," it means that even within a single finger-joint and so forth, one can give rise to immeasurable atoms;
how much more so for the entire body and the like? As for the phrase "external wind":
This refers to the winds from the east and west. Regarding the phrase "coming and going through coarse apertures," this refers to the inhalation and exhalation passing through the posterior opening.

Regarding the phrase "that which is followed by the collection of winds," this refers to the various winds that come and go through the pores, circulating throughout the body. Regarding the phrase "that which is encompassed by the collection of winds," [it refers to the winds contained within the body].

The winds within the pores belong to that outer wheel; thus it is said that "the wind-treasury is hidden," because the winds within the pores are difficult to perceive. As for the phrase "immeasurable masses of wind" and so forth:
As stated above, because the three kinds of wind-aggregates all gather within the body of that practitioner, a second analogy is established;
thus the treatise says: "like soiled cotton and the like. Regarding the phrase "or while not yet dead," etc.:
This refers to the fact that one who has entered the attainment of cessation lacks inhalation and exhalation.

Regarding the phrase "pervading all," it means when one practices the meditation on counting breaths based on the category of reliance, the category of contemplation, and the category of non-distraction.

The contemplation of the merit of the stage of cessation characterized by signlessness, as well as the contemplation that the inhalations and exhalations are ever-new and not old, should be explained here just as in the previous section on the contemplation of impurity;
this is because the meaning is identical, and thus it refers back to the preceding text. As for the phrase "abiding in the blazing," etc.:
This means that when practicing the five contemplations, such as that on impurity, one practices them with intense application and diligent effort.
Regarding "constant cultivation," it refers to practicing without interruption within the country. Regarding "ultimate cultivation," it refers to...
This means that one practices with ultimate persistence regarding the fruit.

Regarding the phrase "by the power of the cause," it means that by taking śamatha and vipaśyanā as the cause, one is able to induce powerful physical and mental pliancy (praśrabdhi). Regarding the phrase "the preceding signs" (pūrvanimitta):

That is to say, when one of the five contemplations is about to achieve accomplishment, a sign of pliancy (praśrabdhi) appears as if one’s own crown were being pressed down by a stone; this is what is meant by the phrase "that which obstructs the abandonment of pleasure."

This means that afflictions such as greed can obstruct the practice of the formative activities for meditating on impurity and so forth. Regarding the statement that the wind element increases predominantly:
it is because pliancy arises from among the five contemplations.
The practitioner’s body and mind are like the wind;

their practice is held without heaviness. To say they are "like being filled to overflowing" means that the pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) produced by the path of the five contemplations pervades the entire body.
Because the contents placed within the bag are so completely full that they appear as if overflowing,
at such a time the practitioner’s body and mind experience states such as exultation. Regarding the phrase "adorned afterwards":
This means that by the power of pliancy (*praśrabdhi*),
the body and mind are adorned and expanded without requiring further effort. As for the statement "gradually subsiding and ceasing," it refers to the fact that within the preceding stage,
states of mind such as exuberance (*pragraha*) are of the nature of attachment (*rāga*).
In this context, all of these are also eliminated;

thus, the treatise states "the practice of tranquility" and so forth. Regarding the phrase "in yoga" and so on, it refers to the period following the complete suffusion of the head by the lightness and pliancy of the winds.
One thereby enters the ranks of those who practice the five contemplations.

As for what is called "the concentration of the form realm," it refers to attaining at least a small portion of the four untainted (*anāsrava*) dhyānas. Regarding the phrase "attaining this mental attention (*manasikāra*) and so forth":
In this regard, there is a question:

what are the characteristics of the four mental orientations (*manasikāra*)—namely, "endowed with the initial stage," "heavy," "tranquil," and "wind-increase-filling"—for a practitioner who has just begun their training?

Therefore, the treatise answers by stating, "one attains these mental orientations," etc. Regarding the phrase, "having already obtained that which is included within the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*)," etc.:
This refers to attaining a small portion [of the path] within the four untainted (*anāsrava*) meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).

Regarding the phrases "possessing power" and "possessing capability," this means possessing the power and capability with respect to the five contemplations on impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) and so forth.
Because they are able to purify and eliminate the five kinds of objects to be countered, such as the characteristic of purity (*śubha-nimitta*) and so forth;
the phrase "all practices" refers to the reversal of these five, beginning with purity; and as for the phrase "even though they arise only slightly," it means...
Just as the contemplation of impurity can eliminate objects that require purification,
so too should one understand that the contemplations of loving-kindness and so forth can treat objects that require cultivation. Regarding the phrase "not longing":
This means not being excessively preoccupied with or craving objects such as sensual desires.

Regarding the phrase "not delighting in anxiety," it means not taking pleasure in [the pursuit of] clothing, food, and so forth, yet giving rise to anxiety regarding them. Regarding the phrase "all the concomitant characteristics,"...
This refers to not delighting in signs such as purity, aversion, and so forth. Regarding the term "not extreme," it is to be applied to each of the subsequent signs.

This concludes the Hand-Copy of the Thirty-second Volume of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*. The third section, the *Pratipatty-yoga-sthāna*, is finished. Regarding the statement "extensively explaining the two meditative attainments":
This refers to the two meditative attainments of signlessness and cessation.

Regarding the "five supernormal powers," these are the fruits of the eight meditative concentrations, namely the eight fundamental stages beginning with the first dhyāna. As for what are called the five supernormal powers:

Regarding "meditative absorption" (*dhyāna*): as for the distinction of birth, it refers to the fact that birth in the first dhyāna and so forth differs in each case. Regarding "the various characteristics":
it refers to the abandonment of desire for both the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) and the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*).
The seven gates above establish the fruits according to the mundane path (*laukikamārga*).

Regarding the phrase "observing the truths," this refers to practitioners of the stage of penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*). Regarding the phrase "thoroughly penetrating as it truly is," this refers to...
This, then, is the stage of the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*). Regarding the detailed analysis of cultivation (*bhāvanā*), it means that this is its cultivation.
