The First Part of the Section on Yoga for Attaining Fruition: An Introductory Discourse.
Regarding the two meditative concentrations (*samādhi*), they shall be explained extensively according to the words of the teachings on merit and wisdom.
This refers to the two meditative attainments of signlessness and cessation.
Regarding the "five supernormal powers," these are the fruits of the eight dhyānas, namely the fundamental stages of the eight dhyānas. Regarding "all signs":
This refers to being free from the desires of the two realms: the desire realm and the form realm.
These seven preceding sections establish the fruits based on the mundane path (*laukikamārga*).

Regarding the phrase "observing the truths," this refers to practitioners who have cultivated the four stages of penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*). Regarding the phrase "penetrating according to reality," it refers to...
"This is the stage of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*). Regarding the statement "extensively analyzing [the path] in cultivation," this refers to the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
Regarding the statement "culmination is its subsequent [stage]," this refers to the final stage.
This refers to the stage of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*). Regarding the phrase "those who delight in abandoning a small portion":

this refers to those who, having first resolved their minds, cultivate the seven types of mental attention (*manasikāra*) and take pleasure in seeing and cultivating the two categories of afflictions. Regarding the phrase "they first cultivate" and "the first," etc.: [this indicates the initial stage].

This means that because ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) have not yet abandoned the two types of afflictions—those of the path of seeing (*darśana-heya*) and those of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*)—they are said to be "not fully bound" by both.

This refers to those in training (*śaikṣa*), who have already abandoned the afflictions of the path of seeing and have partially abandoned the afflictions of the path of cultivation. Regarding the phrase "and so forth, up to," [it indicates the inclusion of further categories].
This means that from the second dhyāna up to the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), there are six [stages].

Regarding the phrase "furthermore, with respect to the dhyānas," it means that the eight meditative absorptions, such as the dhyānas, serve as the cause for being able to induce the two mindless attainments—the cessation attainment (*nirodhasamāpatti*)—and the five supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
Thus, it refers to the divine eye and so forth.
"If it is birth" refers to the sixth section on the distinctions of birth mentioned previously.
"If it is characteristics" refers to the seventh section on the characteristics of detachment from desire mentioned previously.
The reason the eighth gate— the observation of the truths (*satya*) and so forth—
is not listed here is that it is subsumed within the causes and fruits of the supramundane path (*lokottaramārga*). As for the term "skeleton" (*asthisaṃkalā*),
this reveals that the five objects of desire (*pañcakāmaguṇa*) are like withered bones.
Although the food lacks flavor, this demonstrates that there is no satiety.
As for the expression "congealed blood," this demonstrates the sense of being shared by many, like a marketplace where many people share in the harm. As for the expression "grass torch,"...
This reveals the meaning of the cause of misconduct:
namely, that one who grasps a grass torch and does not let go will surely burn their hand.
As for the phrase "a portion of charcoal fire," this reveals the increase of craving.
If one approaches a pit of fire, it cannot quench thirst.
As for the mention of "venomous snakes," this reveals the meaning of what the wise person keeps at a distance. As for the mention of "what is seen in a dream":
This reveals the meaning of swiftly proceeding toward extinction.
The phrase "borrowing ornaments" reveals the meaning of relying upon various conditions (*pratyaya*). The phrase "like the tip of a tree" [reveals...]
This reveals the meaning that negligence endangers the sixth stage (*ṣaṣṭhī bhūmi*).
That is to say, those who indulge in sensual desires will inevitably fall into the evil destinies (*apāya*).

Regarding the phrase "and so forth," the meaning of these eight similes has already been explained in detail within the *Mīmāṃsā-gāthā* of the *Cintāmayī Bhūmi*. Regarding the phrase "these various sensual desires and so forth":
Within these sixteen lines,
the first eight correspond one-to-one with the preceding eight similes;
the latter eight reveal the faults of desire by relying on [the teaching of] impermanence and so forth.

As should be understood from the treatise: the phrase "this attention and so forth" means that the subsequent superior resolve-attention (*adhimokṣa-manasikāra*) arises with the attention that discerns characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-pratividhi-manasikāra*) as its cause. Regarding the term "intermingled": [it refers to their alternating occurrence].
This refers to the attention characterized by accomplishment (*niṣpanna-manasikāra*), which is achieved through the alternating cultivation of the two methods of hearing and reflection.

The statement "using only cultivation" indicates that one relies on the aspect of wisdom born of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mayī-prajñā*) to take the object of the first dhyāna as its focal point. The statement "this very [attention] consisting of resolute conviction (*adhimukti*)," and so forth, [is explained as follows].
This means that because the three superior resolves—at the beginning, middle, and end—act as causes, one accomplishes the subsequent attention of detachment;
thus, the treatise states, "first arising," and so forth. As for the phrase "concomitant attention":
This refers to the time when one abandons the coarse characteristics of afflictions in the desire realm, occurring simultaneously with mental attention (*manasikāra*).
In the following five sections, each subsequent phenomenon is established by taking the preceding one as its cause. Regarding the phrase "all afflictions":
This refers to the manifestation of hindrances within the first dhyāna.
The term "coarseness" (*dausthulya*) refers to the absence of pliancy (*praśrabdhi*). Regarding the phrase "from this point onward," etc.:
This means that through the mental application of seclusion (*viveka-manasikāra*), one cultivates seven factors as the causes for the arising of joy; only then is seclusion truly accomplished.
First, delighting in abandonment (*prahāṇa-rati*);
second, delighting in seclusion (*viveka-rati*).
Third, one perceives the superior merits within all forms of abandonment.
Fourth, one touches upon and realizes a small portion [of the goal],
namely, because one has for the first time attained the bliss of being free from birth (*vivekaja-prīti*).
Fifth, at times, the mental orientation of joyful interest;
sixth, at times, the mental orientation of disenchantment;
seventh, for the purpose of abandoning the five hindrances that obstruct the first dhyāna.
Therefore, the treatise states, "in order to eliminate," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "cultivating proximity" and so on, this refers to the three stages of mind—initial, middle, and final.
This means that within the obstacles to the first dhyāna, one has not yet been able to sever various types of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).
Because one gives rise to delusion upon seeing pure and wondrous forms and so forth, the treatise states that "one is unable to relinquish them" and so on.
The phrase "all conditioned phenomena" (*saṃskāra*) refers to the conditioned phenomena of form and the rest. The phrase "this is due to being merely temporary" and so forth means:
In this regard, there is an objection:
when one eliminates the coarse characteristics of the desire realm through the concentration of the first dhyāna,
is it able to eliminate the seeds that have existed for a long time all at once?
Does this mean that only the active manifestations (*samudācāra*) are severed?
Therefore, the treatise answers: "This is due to being temporary," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "Furthermore, with regard to detachment," etc., there is a question here.

Among the seven modes of mental attention (*manasikāra*), why is it that only the four beginning with "separation" (*viveka*) are explained as having the characteristic of experiencing pleasure (*sukha-vedanā*),
while the other three are not? Answer:

Because these three types of mental attention (*manasikāra*) are observed through the resolution of signs (*nimitta-adhimokṣa*), they are said to belong to the state of non-concentration (*asamāhita-bhūmi*) during the period of distraction; therefore, they cannot produce bliss. Regarding the phrase "without interval": it means that there is no gap [between them].
This means that from the moment one has attained [this state] until the end of life, the joy and bliss born of seclusion are uninterrupted. Regarding the "five factors":
first, vitarka;
second, vicāra.
Third is joy;
fourth is bliss;
fifth is one-pointedness of mind. Regarding the phrase "abiding in the desire realm," etc.:
This is because it serves as the antidote to the coarse characteristics of the desire realm and enables the cultivation and realization of the fruit of the first dhyāna.
Regarding this, a question arises:

among the seven types of mental attention (*manaskāra*), why is it that only the "mental attention that discerns characteristics" (*lakṣaṇapratisaṃvedī-manaskāra*) and so forth are explicitly mentioned?
This means that the five desires should be abandoned and the first dhyāna should be attained. Regarding the statement "one is able [to recognize] what has been attained" and so forth:

if one does not investigate, one gives rise to the perception of attainment regarding what has not yet been attained; this is called overweening pride (*adhimāna*). Regarding the statement "furthermore, if one understands the characteristics" and so forth:

This means that these two dharmas collectively accord with the cultivation of revulsion toward the five desires and the practice of their remedies. Regarding the phrase "and so forth" (*ādi*), according to the Tibetan version, it says:
It should be understood that these six types of mental attention are subsumed within four types of mental attention;
herein, it is intended to exclude the mental attention that is the fruit of the culmination of application.

The remaining six are all included within the four dharmas such as "conformity" (anuloma) and so forth, because they are mental orientations (manasikāra) belonging to the stage of a cause. Regarding the phrase "according to the respective stages," this refers to the first dhyāna.
The coarse aspect (*audārikatva*) of the first dhyāna and the pure aspect (*śubhatva*) of the second dhyāna are to be understood through the meaning of mutual dependence (*apekṣā*).

The principles for the remaining three should be known by analogy with what precedes. Regarding the phrase "should be known as before": it means they are to be understood in accordance with the aforementioned method.

Just as the attention that discerns characteristics (*lakṣaṇapratisaṃvedī manaskāra*) pervades the entire first dhyāna, so too do the six [mental applications], beginning with that of resolute conviction (*adhimokṣika*), likewise pervade it.
Therefore, as previously stated, the phrase "the first dhyāna" and the subsequent phrase "furthermore, among these... [are used].
If one follows the Tibetan version,
the scriptural passages are first presented,
followed by their explanation.
Regarding the scriptural passages within this interval,
the expounder should understand them as follows. As for what are called "scriptural passages," the Sūtra says:
The first dhyāna means being secluded from sensual desires and unwholesome states;
it possesses applied and sustained thought, and is born of seclusion, characterized by joy and bliss.
One fully dwells in this first dhyāna. As for the term "afflictive desire":
This refers to the mutual passion and attachment between men and women.
"Desire for objects" refers to craving for wealth, treasures, and the like.
"Detachment from association" refers to the meaning of being free from association with the five sensory desires. "Detachment from objective spheres" refers to...
This refers to the objects of the five desires (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*).
What is called "affliction" (*kleśa*) refers to the desire of affliction;
what is called "desire" (*kāma*) refers to the desire for things. Regarding the phrase "having this as the cause":
This means that it is due to the *prayoganiṣṭha-manasikāra* (the mental application of the culmination of the preparatory stage) serving as the cause.

Regarding the phrase "by means of what has been cultivated," this refers to the accomplishment of the fruit of the culmination of the preparatory stage. Regarding the phrase "attaining according to one's wish," [it refers to the attainment of the desired goal].
This means that one attains mastery over entering, emerging, and so forth.
Regarding "difficulty," it means that with little cultivation, one is able to bring oneself into correspondence with meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Regarding "obstruction" (*kaṣāya*),...
"Stem" (*kaṅkha*) is a term for abbreviation;

it means that because no effort is required, one says that the mind is able to be correct throughout the entire night. This is to be understood as corresponding respectively to each of the three minds, beginning with "conformity" (*anuloma*). Regarding the phrase "according to what is desired": [it refers to the practitioner's own aspiration].

This means that those who have definitely attained [this concentration] within the desire realm are able to emerge from that concentration only after seven days. Regarding the phrase "furthermore, concerning those with vitarka," if one follows the Tibetan version:
Regarding each of these four dhyānas, first the scriptural passage is cited,
and only afterwards is it explained.
That is to say, both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna sūtras state:
The second dhyāna is so called because of the subsiding of applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*),
because of internal serenity,
and because of one-pointedness of mind.
"Born of concentration, joy and bliss;
he dwells fully established in the second dhyāna. Regarding the phrase "he accomplishes this and that," the Sūtra says:
Regarding the "third dhyāna":
based on this freedom from desire, one dwells in equanimity, with right mindfulness and right clear comprehension, experiencing bodily pleasure;
the noble ones declare it to be endowed with equanimity, mindfulness, and clear comprehension.
Abiding in the body and experiencing bliss, he dwells fully established in the third dhyāna, free from joy;
the explanation of the meaning is as in the treatise. As for the term "joy" (prīti):
This is the second distracted mind. What is called "a mind contrary to joy" refers to the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*).
What is called the "form-body" refers to the five physical sense-faculties (*pañca-rūpīndriyāṇi*). What is called the "mind" (*manas*) refers to...
The faculty of mind (*manas-indriya*). Regarding the phrase "the third dhyāna and above," these two gates explain the various causes.
Regarding the phrase "lower stages," this refers to those from the second dhyāna downward.
Regarding the phrase "higher stages," [this refers to those above].
This refers to that which is above the fourth dhyāna. "The noble ones" refers to the Buddha and his noble disciples.
According to the Tibetan version, this section should include both the departure from joy and the full dwelling in the third dhyāna.
Since the explanation of the meaning is the same as before, the translator has not provided it here;
the speaker should understand this. Regarding the phrase "Furthermore," etc., there is an objection herein.
For what reason does the Sūtra, within the context of the fourth dhyāna, speak only of the abandonment of pleasure and not of its antidote?
Therefore, the Śāstra answers: "In this context, [it refers to] the antidote, etc."

This means that because the antidote for abandoning pleasure is similar to the previously mentioned antidotes for abandoning applied thought (*vitarka*), sustained thought (*vicāra*), and joy (*prīti*),
it is not explicitly stated here. In this context,
the scriptural passage previously cited should likewise be combined [with the current explanation].
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"As for what is called the fourth dhyāna,
it is because of the abandonment of pleasure."
Because suffering has been abandoned,
prior sorrow and joy have subsided;
at that time, he dwells in equanimity and mindfulness, pure and free from both suffering and pleasure.
He dwells fully established in the fourth dhyāna.

The explanation of the terms is as follows: "that which was previously abandoned" refers to the feeling of joy (*prīti*), the feeling of sorrow (*daurmanasya*), and the feeling of suffering (*duḥkha*); "that which is now abandoned" refers to...
This refers to the pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*) that is abandoned in the fourth dhyāna. Regarding the phrase "now, based on this middle [state]," there is a question here:
if the pleasant feeling is abandoned in the fourth meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), [how is it so?]
Why does the Sūtra state that the fourth dhyāna also abandons the three—suffering, joy, and grief?
Therefore, the Śāstra answers: "In this context, it is equal.
Although suffering and pleasure are abandoned, it is termed the sensation of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*).

Because joy (*prīti*) and sorrow (*daurmanasya*) were previously abandoned during the cultivation of the first, second, and third dhyānas, they are here collectively described as being abandoned in the fourth. As for the mention of blue, yellow, red, white, and so forth:

This refers to the form (*rūpa*) of the two realms, namely the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the form realm (*rūpadhātu*). As for the term "detachment from desire" (*vītarāga*), it means the loathing of the desires of the form realm.
If one follows the Fanben (the Tibetan manuscript), one should likewise first cite the scriptural passage.
The Sūtra says:
"As for what is called the Sphere of Infinite Space,
it is so called because the characteristics of form have been transcended."
Because the characteristic of resistance has ceased and vanished,
and because one does not attend to various characteristics,
one enters the sphere of infinite space.
Regarding the phrase "fully abiding in the sphere of infinite space," the expression "various categories" refers to the blue,
yellow, and so forth within the desire and form realms, all of which arise from the combination of shape and color.
It is capable of creating obstacles within the formless realm (*ārūpya*). Regarding the phrase "by means of detachment" and so forth:
although food, drink, and the like do not exist within the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), there are nonetheless palaces, clothing, and articles of adornment.
Therefore, it is called "the characteristic of equality" (*samatā-lakṣaṇa*). As for the phrase "Furthermore, if by means of equality," the Sūtra says:
"Regarding what is called the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*)."

Having transcended the sphere of infinite space, one enters the sphere of infinite consciousness and dwells fully established in the sphere of infinite consciousness. Regarding the phrase "Furthermore, from the sphere of infinite consciousness," etc.:
The Sūtra says:
"It is called 'nothingness' because it transcends everything, including the sphere of infinite consciousness and the sphere of nothingness."
One fully dwells in the sphere of nothingness.

This means that, due to the cause of being weary of the sphere of infinite consciousness, one gives rise to resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*) regarding the sphere of nothingness. As for the statement "or form": [it refers to the following].
The aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*).
That which is called "non-form" refers to the remaining four aggregates.

That which is called "all that exists" means that within the aforementioned meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), no characteristics—whether with characteristics, without characteristics, or neither with nor without characteristics—can be apprehended.
Therefore, the text of the treatise says, "it is not characterized by signs" (*animitta*), and "it is not like non-existence" (*na-asad-ādi*).
This means that in all states of mind, the concentration on the signless (*animitta-samādhi*) extinguishes the first six consciousnesses.
If there are two types of the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*):
when a non-returner (*anāgāmin*) enters it, the seventh consciousness and those below are ceased;
when an arhat enters it, the eighth consciousness is ceased. As for the phrase "within honey":
Just as it is difficult for bees and the like to find honey within [the hive],
so too is supramundane concentration.
Therefore, the Tibetan version says:
"His physical form sinks into the earth.

Regarding the term "equal," it means that while the signless concentration (*animitta-samādhi*) can be entered by relying on the four dhyānas, the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) can be entered by relying on the four formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*). Regarding the phrase "temporarily ceasing," etc.:
This means that because the two phenomena of perception (*saṃjñā*) and feeling (*vedanā*) disturb the body and mind, they are temporarily stilled.
What is called the "object" (*ālambana*) refers to these two phenomena of perception and feeling. What is called "non-attention" (*amanasikāra*) refers to...

This means not being mindful of those perceptions. Regarding the phrase "the state where the mind exists," it refers to the time when one cultivates the six types of attention, such as the perception of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjanakāra-samjñā*) and so forth;
at these times, the sixth mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is present. Regarding the phrase "the mind no longer turns back," it means...
This refers to the stage of the ultimate fruit of the seventh preparatory application (*prayoga*).

Regarding the statement "the mind and mental factors cease," it means that the sixth consciousness and those below it, along with their associated [factors], no longer function. Regarding the term "fundamental" (*maula*):
This refers to the mental attention that is the fruit of the culmination of the preparatory application for the four dhyānas.

Regarding the phrase "knowing by way of the meaning," this refers to the principles of the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*). Regarding the phrase "knowing by way of the Dharma," [it refers to...]
This refers to the knowledge of the causal and resultant dharmas of the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*).
Regarding the phrase "at times," it means that those of dull faculties cultivate the twelve characteristics, such as levitation and so forth, within this very life.
Only in a subsequent birth can one truly give rise to the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*). Regarding the term "possessing parts" (*sabhāga*):

it refers to those of sharp faculties who, by practicing in this very life, are able to give rise to the characteristics of the five supernormal powers. Regarding the term "this perception" (*saṃjñā*): [it refers to...]
This means that by means of buoyancy, one gives rise to the perception of the resolve for buoyancy regarding the body.
The meaning of the following nine categories is identical to this. As for the term "proficiency":

This refers to silk cloth. Regarding the phrase "and so forth in the detailed explanation," it should be understood that this applies equally to the meditative resolution (*adhimukti*) regarding the transformation of earth and water into the characteristics of wind and fire, and vice versa.
Therefore, the treatise says "extensively explained" and so forth. Regarding the phrase "or with his body," it means by way of accomplishing the characteristics of the space element (*ākāśadhātu*).
Regarding the phrase "or in that ground," etc. [it refers to the accomplishment of the characteristics of the earth element].
This is because of the accomplishment of the characteristics of being supple, light, and buoyant.
Regarding the phrase "or in the vast," etc., this is due to the accomplishment of the harmony between body and mind, and so forth. Regarding the phrase "as appropriate," [it refers to]...
The above four signs correspond respectively to each [of the four elements].
That is to say, by virtue of the resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*) that apprehends the characteristics of the space element (*ākāśadhātu*),
one passes straight through walls and other such obstacles without impediment.
All other cases should be understood according to this principle. Regarding the phrase "a portion":

this refers to the interval from the desire realm up to the intermediate state of the first dhyāna, where there exist only the derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*) of spirits and the like, which cannot constitute an obstruction. Regarding the phrase "by these [factors]": [it refers to the aforementioned causes].
This means that by virtue of accomplishing the characteristic of recollection,
one is able to know the sequence of one's own activities from birth to old age without losing their order, even within the coarse aspect of the phenomena.
One cannot recollect subtle characteristics;
that is to say, through the mundane path, one can recollect both the coarse and the subtle.
This demonstrates the supernormal power of knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna-abhijñā*). Regarding the phrase "and furthermore, regarding various [characteristics]," etc.:

That which can clearly understand the functional capacity of all wholesome and unwholesome karma of sentient beings within the five destinies to produce good and evil fruits is also called the characteristic of light.
As for the phrase "the color of constant change":
This means that when one is angry, if one offends another, the other's facial expression changes. Regarding the phrase "to be explained in detail, up to... and so forth:
it refers to the various modes of transformation in all sentient beings according to their respective afflictions, such as greed and the like.
This is called the supernormal power of knowing the minds of others (*paracittajñānābhijñā*).
Regarding what is called the supernormal power of transforming things (*vastuvikārābhijñā*), it refers to such acts as transforming earth into water and so forth.

Regarding what is called the supernormal power of creating things (*nirmāṇābhijñā*), it refers to making that which does not exist appear as if it were present. Regarding what is called "resolute conviction" (*adhimukti*):
This refers to such things as transforming the small into the great and so forth.

As for "the absence of conflict," it refers to the *araṇā-samādhi* (the concentration of non-conflict), because it brings forth sentient beings. As for "knowledge resulting from aspiration" (*praṇidhijñāna*),...
This refers to the vast practices and vows.
The rest of the text is self-evident. Regarding the phrase "Wen-sheng" (文聖) and so forth:
although the supernormal power of the divine realm (*ṛddhividhi-jñāna*) is discussed herein, [the following applies].
Regarding the statement that "all five powers possess distinctions yet are all capable of accomplishment":
this means that while the first five characteristics can accomplish the supernormal power of psychic travel (*ṛddhividhi-jñāna*),
the remaining five also all possess the capacity for accomplishment.
As previously stated, "mixed cultivation" refers to the simultaneous cultivation of both mundane and supramundane paths. Regarding the phrase "in which place," among the three grades,
the sphere of emptiness (*ākāśāyatana*) and the sphere of consciousness (*vijñānāyatana*) are combined as the lower grade.
The remaining two are superior. Regarding the phrase "by those various devas and so forth," there is a question here:
do these [heavens] have a specific location, or are they without a specific location? They lack the four dhyānas. Are they with a location or without a location?
Therefore, the treatise answers that there is no color, shape, or the like.

Although there is no location, it is designated by specific names based on its functions, such as emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*). As for the phrase "within this very [state], the inferior grade, etc.":
That is to say, by taking these five categories as causes, one realizes rebirth in the five Śuddhāvāsa heavens.
The hand-copied notes for the thirty-third fascicle of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* are complete.
Hand-copied notes for the thirty-fourth fascicle of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.

In discussing the practice of impermanence regarding merit and wisdom, it means that all internal and external conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) arise and perish. Regarding the practice of suffering,
it means...
It is called "the nature of oppression" because it is the practice of emptiness;
it is called "the practice of non-self" because it contradicts the view of self;
and it is called "that which leads by cause" because it contradicts the view of self.
This means that karma and afflictions are the factors capable of producing [existence].
It is called "accumulating" because it has many varieties; it is called "arousing and drawing forth" because it constantly produces assets; it is called "conditioning" because...
It is called "the practice of cessation" because it is the individual assistance [that brings an end to suffering].
It is called "the practice of tranquility" because the various aggregates (*skandha*) have been exhausted.
It is called "the practice of excellence" because the three characteristics, such as birth and old age, have subsided.
Because it is free from all afflictions, it is called "the practice of detachment.
Because it is liberated from all calamities, it is called "the practice of the path.
Because it has the sense of universal application, it is called "the practice of suchness."
Because they accord with correct principle, they are called "practitioners.
Because they proceed correctly toward [the goal], they are called "those who go forth.
Because they are able to transcend forever, they are called "those who dwell for a long time."
This refers to the period from when the kalpa has already been destroyed at its end. As for the term "Seven-Day Sūtra," it is the name of a sūtra of the Hīnayāna;
that sūtra explains in detail the time when the three realms are destroyed.
This is because they manifest all at once over seven days.
"Not turning away" means that what is directly perceived is not hidden.
"Not depending on other conditions" means that because it is direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), one sees it without requiring the pointing out of another person. As for "all the radiances":
This refers to the light of the sun and so forth. Regarding the phrase "a portion of states," it refers to the transformations of the eight stages.
Regarding the term "defilement," it refers to the transformations caused by various afflictions such as greed.
Regarding the phrase "referring to the experience of pleasant sensation and so forth," [it refers to the conditions for that sensation].
This refers to the clear manifestation of transformation within the three types of sensation (*vedanā*).

Regarding the phrase "furthermore, there is convergence," etc., this refers to the establishment of transformation based upon the afflictions (*kleśa*). Regarding the phrase "likewise, eye-consciousness," etc., [it refers to the same].
This refers to the clear transformation within the six consciousnesses. Regarding the phrase "or produced by persons," it means that enemies and the like cause harm.
Regarding the phrase "the rest is as previously explained," it refers back to what was stated before.
This refers to the two gates of "interrogation" and "response," which are the same as the previously mentioned "gates of functional states. Regarding "sweet water":
this refers to sweet and delicious water;
this water is like wine in that it can benefit those who are aged or ill. Regarding "those who sacrifice themselves for profit": [this refers to those who pursue gain at any cost].
This refers to seeking, managing, and so forth. Regarding the phrase "the rest as previously explained," it means that the interrogation and response are the same as those explained before.
Regarding the phrase "those various forms, formations, and so forth," [it refers to the aforementioned categories].
This refers to the fact that although all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*)— whether internal or external— arise spontaneously without depending on causes and conditions,
their destruction and impermanence are subtle in nature and are not perceived by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
It is only by relying on inference (*anumāna*) that one can perceive [this];

therefore, the third [chapter] clarifies inference. Within the establishment of the meaning of arising and ceasing, it is said: "Those conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) must possess momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*), etc."
This refers to the various non-Buddhists who cling to the notion that atoms, the *pradhāna* (primordial nature), and so forth, are eternal;

as well as a certain class of followers within our own tradition who cling to the view that internal and external conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) remain eternally stable for three or six moments, and so on.
This means that such erroneous and deviant attachments are refuted;

thus the treatise says, "namely, those conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) and so forth. As for the phrase "not abiding in this way," it refers to the reality of internal and external dependent origination.
If [you claim that] arising occurs from atoms, supreme nature (*prakṛti*), or other such [causes], this is not the case.
Since their essence would be eternal, there would be no distinction between before and after;
yet, because change, arising, and ceasing are perceptible, [your claim] that "once arisen, it does not depend on causes and conditions for destruction" is untenable.
This refers to all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) produced through internal and external dependent origination.
At the time of their arising, they arise only by depending upon and relying on causes and conditions;
at the time of their disintegration, they perish naturally without depending on causes and conditions.
Just as when people of this world throw a stone into the air, they rely on human effort;

yet at the moment the stone falls, it does not rely on human exertion but falls spontaneously—this principle is likewise so in these refutations. Regarding the phrase "all such causes and conditions for transformation," etc.:
In this regard, there is an objection:
if there is no cause for the cessation of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) produced by internal and external conditions,
then do not the eight types of causes for transformation mentioned previously constitute the causes for their destruction?
Therefore, the treatise answers with the words, "All such as these," and so forth.

The intended meaning here is that the eight kinds of transformation previously established are the causes and conditions for the arising of transformation within internal and external dependent origination; they are not causes for destruction.
Just as a hammer breaking a jar is the cause of its disintegration and not the cause for the destruction of its atoms,

the principle herein is likewise. As for the statement that "both are destroyed," it means that once the causes and conditions of internal and external dependent origination have both been destroyed, [the result ceases].
Subsequently, it is through dissimilar activity that transformation (vipariṇāma) arises.
Therefore, these eight kinds of causes for transformation are causes of arising, not causes of cessation.
If they were causes of cessation, [transformation would not occur].
Just as when the characteristics of youth perish, the characteristics of that person cannot logically continue to exist; yet they do exist.

Therefore, one should know that the eight kinds of transformation are causes for arising, not causes for cessation. As for the statement, "Or there are certain conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), etc.": [it means that these transformations occur even while the continuum persists].
This is the statement of the position.
The meaning of the objection is as follows:

although these eight kinds of causes for transformation are the causes for the arising of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) produced by internal and external conditions, they are not the causes for their destruction.
This does not constitute a universal principle. Why is this?
Because in the world, there are certain conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) that perish simultaneously with their causes and do not undergo further arising.
It is like fire boiling water:

when the vessel and its contents are consumed by fire, both the world of vessels (*bhājanaloka*) and its causes perish together, for there is no further arising. As for the statement "those [causes] are also dependent origination," etc., this refers to the refutation of the preceding argument regarding causes and analogies.
The intent here is to clarify that the functional capacity and efficacy of fire consists in boiling water and incinerating the vessel-world;
it does not possess the function of exhausting water and so forth.
Therefore, your statement that a portion of the conditioned perishes simultaneously with its cause is unreasonable.
Thus, the treatise says: "It is not by means of fire and so forth. As for the term "the other world":
This refers to the two time periods of the past and the future.
The phrase "all such as these" refers to the sevenfold distinctions, such as superior, inferior, good, and evil. The phrase "previously existing," etc., [refers to...]

This means that because the cause ceases and the effect arises in the same moment, if the Sovereign (Īśvara) existed prior [to the effect], the definition of a "cause" would not be established. Regarding the "three types of predominance":
it is said that initial pure faith is the authoritative scripture (*āgama*).
The remaining two—direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*)—should be understood as explained in the treatise.

Regarding the phrase "for the sake of" (*yasyārtham*), it means that [the preceding] is joined one by one with each of the four subsequent passages. Regarding the phrase "regression and loss" (*parihāṇi*):
This also corresponds one-to-one with each of the four subsequent passages, namely:
the loss of the nature of mastery and so forth. Regarding "the performance of regretful action," it refers to not properly guarding [the mind]. Regarding "the nature of phenomena" (*dharmatā*),...

This means that because the three modes of activity, such as transformation and so forth, are established by the principle of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā-yukti*), they necessarily function as designations (*prajñapti*).
For example, just as a stone thrown into the air must inevitably fall, the principle herein is likewise.
Regarding the phrase "unintentional activity" (*anabhisandhi-pravṛtti*) and so forth:
This means that because painful feeling accords with and enters into the various aggregates of suffering (*duḥkha-skandha*), it enters into the practice of suffering;
therefore, the subsequent passage says, "the aggregates that accord with suffering," and so forth. As for the phrase "unstable conduct" (*an-āśvāsa-carita*):
This means that it is due to the instability of the suffering inherent in conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*).

Regarding the phrase "with outflows" (*sāsrava*) and "with grasping" (*sopādāna*), this refers to the feelings that are neither painful nor pleasant (*aduḥkhāsukha-vedanā*) upon which [the mind] depends. Regarding the phrase "conducive to neither pain nor pleasure," etc.:

This refers to the basis upon which sensation depends. To say "there is only that view" means there is only the view of eternalism, nihilism, and so forth, and not [the views of] self, person, and so forth. To say "its own characteristic" (svalakṣaṇa) means...
This refers to the respective specific characteristics (svalakṣaṇa) of earth, water, and so forth. Regarding the statement that craving can induce suffering and so on:
it means that because karma and afflictions serve as causes, they are able to induce the fruits of suffering within the three realms.
The three subsequent passages are all established on the basis of karma and afflictions. Regarding the term "capable of grasping" (*parigraha*):
it means that craving (*tṛṣṇā*) is able to receive the seeds of all suffering. Regarding the term "inducing" (*ākṣepa*): [it refers to the power of projecting future existence].

This means that the four factors of dependent origination through causes and conditions are all capable of summoning the fruit of suffering within the five destinies. Regarding the phrase "taking up causes," it refers to the three types of craving.
Regarding the phrase "summoning and gathering," [it refers to the process by which these factors bring about rebirth].
This means that grasping conditions existence within the three realms. Regarding the term "foremost," it refers to birth.
Regarding the phrase "birth as a condition," it means that because of birth, there is old age, death, and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "thoroughly understanding," etc., [it refers to the knowledge of these things as they truly are].
This means that craving is called the latent tendency (*anuśaya*) of affliction. Regarding the "basis," it refers to the aggregates (*skandha*) of the five destinies;
for this latent tendency of craving takes the aggregates of the five destinies as its basis.
Because it gathers and brings forth the dharmas that serve as conditions for the future,
the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the afflictions are the causes that bring about [the result],
while the three types of conditions that arise and accumulate are the dharmas that are brought about. As for what is called "the entanglements (*paryavasthāna*) that are produced":
This refers to the three types of craving for future existence (*punarbhava-tṛṣṇā*) and so forth, which will be explained below.

Since these three types of entanglements (*paryavasthāna*) arise from the previously mentioned latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), they are said to be "produced by them. As for the phrase "three types": [it refers to the following].

This refers to the aforementioned afflictions (*kleśa*), latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), and the three types of craving (*tṛṣṇā*). Regarding the "objects of knowledge" (*jñeya-viṣaya*), these refer to the truths of suffering, origin, and cessation.
Because of right view and so forth, one is able to thoroughly investigate and seek out the faults of saṃsāra and the merits of nirvāṇa. As for the "four gates":

This means that the Path, like its practice and emergence, is able to function accordingly through the distancing [of defilements] by means of right view and the other factors. As for the term "inference" (anumāna), it refers to what is called "dissimilar" (asabhāga).
This refers to the two upper realms (*dhātu*). Regarding "inferential" (*anumāna*):
it means that within the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), one contemplates suffering through the five modes of impermanence;
whereas in the two upper realms, there is the impermanence of transformation (*vipariṇāma-anityatā*) and the impermanence of separation (*viveka-anityatā*).
Regarding the impermanence of aggregation (*saṃnipāta-anityatā*), one portion extends into the higher realms;

however, there is only the impermanence of disintegration (*vināśa-anityatā*) and one portion of the impermanence of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā-anityatā*). Furthermore, the sixteen types of external impermanence and the fifteen types of internal impermanence do not exist in the higher realms.
Among the three aspects of suffering, in the higher realms there is only the suffering of instability (*aniśceṣa-duḥkha*).
The aspects of emptiness and non-self are the same as in the desire realm.
Within the truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*), in the higher realms there is no hatred (*dveṣa*).

The others are to be understood by analogy with the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). The aspects (*ākāra*) of cessation (*nirodha*) and the path (*mārga*) are also to be inferred by analogy with those of the desire realm. Regarding the phrase "all that exists" and so forth:

this means that the two truths of suffering (*duḥkha*) and origin (*samudaya*) pervade the higher realms. Regarding the term "in all their modes" (*sarvākāra*): [it refers to the fact that they exist in every aspect].
The higher realms also possess the seeds of immovable karma.
"At all times" refers to the three periods of time [past, present, and future].
"Such phenomena" refers to the phenomena of suffering and its origin. "Such principles" refers to...
This refers to the principle of cause and effect regarding suffering and its origin.
As for the phrase "abiding thus," it means that the two truths of suffering and its origin are, by nature, defiled. As for the phrase "whatever path," [it refers to the truth of cessation].
Within the Noble Eightfold Path, the realms of the higher spheres lack right livelihood and right action;
the remaining factors are the same as those in the desire realm.

As for the phrase "if a practitioner," it means that they have attained certainty regarding the sixteen practices of contemplation within the desire realm. As for the phrase "furthermore, regarding the various truths," it means...
This refers to the arising of resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*) regarding the truths within the two higher realms.

As for the "Dharma that has been taught," it refers to the aforementioned seven kinds of boundless phenomena, beginning with impermanence. As for the phrase "there is nothing further remaining," etc.:

This means that before the Noble Path has yet manifested, one has already expressed that there is no other dharma capable of serving as a skillful means to extinguish birth and death. As for the phrase "furthermore, regarding such [matters]":

This means that a practitioner who employs attention through resolute conviction (adhimokṣa-manasikāra) is able to feel profound weariness and fear toward the three realms of existence and the four modes of birth;
these refer to the two truths of suffering and its origin. As for the phrase "and so forth" (ādi):
This refers to the two truths of cessation and the path.

Regarding the phrase "practicing one mode of rejoicing," it means that among the four modes of each of the two truths—cessation and path—one takes up one of them with a heart of aspiration and delight. Regarding the phrase "he, throughout the long night," and so forth:

This means that because the seeds of the five sensory objects have been nurtured, increased, and accumulated since beginningless time, although one may delight in *nirvāṇa*, the mind may still regress. Regarding the statement, "one thinks as follows, not [as] equal," etc.:
This is precisely what constitutes the conceit of "I. As for the statement that one will "further transmigrate," it means that if there is no antidote, one will continue to transmigrate;
however, because of the antidote of "I," one will no longer transmigrate.
"These twelve kinds of dharmas belong to me alone;
that others lack them is called the growth of the conceit 'I am'. Regarding the phrase "penetrating with wisdom": it means...
This refers to the knowledge of the category of suffering and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "objects of knowledge external [to the self]," this refers to the five and twelve types of *asmimāna* (the conceit "I am"). Regarding the phrase "as they arise," and so forth:
When that practitioner contemplates the Four Noble Truths of the higher realms,
whatever obstructive phenomena arise as previously described are immediately extinguished through the power of their antidotes.
The second dharma refers to the uninterrupted arising of the mind of antidote;
it is said to be of two kinds: first, the dharmas of the aggregates (skandha).
"Because of the relinquishing of the two—self and phenomena.
"Sublime wisdom" refers to the wisdom capable of contemplating the sixteen aspects (*ṣoḍaśākāra*).
"The arising of right knowledge" refers to the arising of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*). "Sublime is the practice," and so forth.
This refers to the eight patiences (*kṣānti*) common to the four truths of the three realms.
When a practitioner who employs attention through resolute conviction (*adhimukti-manasikāra*) attains the samādhi of the eight inferior patiences,
they generate the non-conceptual wisdom of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) by the power of that samādhi.
It is called the "mild stage" (*mṛdu-avasthā*) because the fire of wisdom first manifests with a mild aspect, burning away the fuel of afflictions and karma from beginningless time.
The stages of "Summit" (*mūrdhan*) and "Patience" (*kṣānti*) should be explained accordingly based on the medium and superior degrees of patience.
Regarding why the eight knowledges (*jñāna*) are not established here:
because the eight knowledges constitute the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*), which is a stage of causal development;
therefore, they are not distinguished separately here.
The eight patiences (*kṣānti*) constitute the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*), as they belong to the stage of fruition;

this is what is clarified herein. Regarding the term "the subject that cognizes" (*ālambaka*), it refers to the wisdom realizing the emptiness of persons (*pudgalanairātmyajñāna*). Regarding the term "the object cognized" (*ālambana*), it refers to...

This refers to the sixteen aspects of the Four Noble Truths. To speak of "observing the mind with application" means that there is a conceptualized image consisting of the sixteen aspects of the Four Noble Truths. To speak of "abiding without application" means...
This refers to the non-conceptual images of the sixteen aspects of the Four Noble Truths.
It is said to be "not ceased" because the seeds of karma and afflictions have not yet been severed; it is said to be "not without an object" because [it takes those truths as its object].

This means that because the image of non-conceptual śamatha appears before one; as for the phrase "not beautiful sleep" and so forth, it refers to when that practitioner abides in uninterrupted concentration.
It is not a state of being intoxicated by the "honey-bee" samādhi;
rather, it is because the path of the dual application of clear discerning wisdom and meditative observation has become manifest. As for the phrase "immediately following this," etc.:
This refers to the attention of withdrawal (*prāvivekya-manasikāra*), which arises immediately after the supreme mundane dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*).
To say "arising of internal attention" means the attention of withdrawal. To say "in their respective order" means:

This means first observing the desire realm, and subsequently observing the sixteen aspects (*ṣoḍaśākāra*) of the two higher realms. Regarding the phrase "directly perceived" (*pratyakṣa*), this refers to the Four Truths (*catuḥsatya*) of the desire realm.
Regarding the phrase "not directly perceived," [this refers to those of the higher realms].
This refers to the two upper realms. Regarding the term "non-conceptual," it refers to the non-conceptual images of the sixteen aspects. Regarding the term "definitive knowledge,"...
This refers to the wisdom of direct perception (*pratyakṣajñāna*). Regarding the phrase "because this is permanently severed," etc.:

if one has already abandoned the nine grades of afflictions of the desire realm through the mundane path (*laukikamārga*), one now enters the clear observation of the truths (*satyābhisamaya*) within this [path] and attains the fruit of non-returner (*anāgāmiphala*). Regarding the phrase "as previously stated," etc.: [it means that] by means of that [previously mentioned]...
That is to say, as previously stated, there are twelve types of persons who have become free from desire through the mundane path;
their characteristics are just as described in the seventh section above,
and this case is likewise so.
If that is so, what is the difference between this and the detachment from desire through the mundane path (*laukikamārga*)?
Therefore, the treatise answers: "However, in this regard, they are equal.
This means that although those who follow the mundane path are born in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), [the distinction remains].
From that nirvana, one may return to be born in the desire realm;
however, if one follows the supramundane path from that nirvana, one then attains the state of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa) and does not return again to be born in the desire realm.

There is this distinction. Regarding the phrase "if one has previously abandoned twice as much" (*dviguṇa-vairāgya*), it refers to the stage [of the path of cultivation] wherein one has severed the first six categories among the nine categories of afflictions of the desire realm. Regarding the phrase "one who is able to know," it refers to...
This means that the wisdom which takes the emptiness of persons as its object is in conjunction with and faces the sixteen aspects (ākāra) of the object.
Regarding the phrase "this is also established," although there are twelve types of characteristics within the mundane path, [the following applies].
This also possesses eighteen kinds of characteristics, because it transcends the mundane path.
"The wisdom that realizes phenomena" refers to the wisdom that understands the emptiness of persons. "The wisdom that is not nihilistic" refers to...
This refers to the stream-enterer’s abandonment of the knowledge of the path of annihilationism.

Regarding the statement "possessing the knowledge of impermanence," this refers to the stream-enterer’s abandonment of the view of eternalism. Regarding the statement "attaining the knowledge of dependent origination":

This means that one realizes dependent origination is like a conjuration appearing crosswise; there is no real self. Regarding the phrase "only one's own dharmas, such as views," this refers to the sequential assignment and explanation of the dharmas of the Four Noble Truths.
Regarding the phrase "the four types of verified clarity" (catvāri avetyaprasādāni):

This refers to the four purities (*catasraḥ pariśuddhayaḥ*): namely, the purity of the Three Jewels, the purity of being beloved by the noble ones (*āryakānta*), the purity of non-affliction (*anāsrava*), and the purity of non-obstruction (*anāvaraṇa*). Regarding the "eighth existence":

this refers to those of the stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*) who possess the most dull faculties; since they attain the state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) after at most seven births, there is no eighth existence for them. Regarding the phrase "the path as it has been attained": [it refers to the realization of the fruit through that very path].
This refers to the sixteen aspects of the Four Noble Truths. Regarding the statement that there are distinctions:
it means that if a stream-enterer gives rise to afflictions, they can only eliminate them through the three grades of antidotes—superior, middling, and inferior.
If this once-returner should give rise to afflictions through a lapse of mindfulness, even a weak counteractive measure is able to dispel them;
thus there is a distinction. As for what is called "superior" (adhimātra):
This refers to the arising of weak and inferior greed toward the objects of the five desires at their highest level.
In contrast, those prior to the first fruit [of stream-entry] give rise to weak greed and so forth even toward objects of an inferior grade.

This is also their distinguishing characteristic. Regarding the phrase "all paths," it refers to everything from the once-returner up to the candidate for arhatship (aśaikṣa-mārga), all of which arise through the three types of mental attention (*manasikāra*): that of delight in cultivation (*prahāṇa-rati*), that of detachment (*viveka*), and that of the culmination of application (*prayoga-niṣṭha*).
Regarding the phrase "correctly cultivating the path already attained," which refers to "by means of the meditative stages (*samāhitabhūmi*) and so forth":
this means that the wisdom arising from the supramundane path is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
Therefore, the wholesome qualities thus cultivated are also called conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
"Increasing" refers to the initial mind;
"uninterrupted" refers to...
"The central mind" refers to the subsequent mind.
Because these three minds cause all the wholesome dharmas that have been cultivated to converge, they are called "excellent wholesome dharmas."
This means that the three liberations and the six supernormal powers are all obtained through the cultivation of the twenty wholesome meditative concentrations.

Regarding the phrase "abiding as before," it refers to abiding in the nine types of practice, as already explained in the section on the yoga of cultivation. Regarding the phrase "cultivation is also as before," etc., [it refers to the same].
This refers to what is taught regarding the four kinds of aspects of cultivation (*bhāvanākāra*) and the cultivation of the bases of yoga (*yogasthāna*).
"Knowledge of exhaustion" (*kṣayajñāna*) refers to the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantaryamārga*);
"knowledge of non-arising" (*anutpādajñāna*) refers to the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*). Regarding the phrase "at that time," and so forth:
This refers to the time of realizing the diamond-like samādhi (*vajropama-samādhi*).
Regarding the phrase "realizing the meaning of mastery," it means that, for example, the Buddhas realize their own objective. Regarding the phrase "abiding in emptiness" and so forth:
This refers to the sequential correlation of the gates of liberation, such as emptiness and so forth.

Regarding the mention of "compassion and so forth," it means that these are cultivated as the causes for the Brahma-abodes (*brahmavihāra*) within the mundane path. Regarding the term "keyhole" (*kavāṭa*), [it refers to...]
This means that because of the pivots of karma and afflictions,
sentient beings are unable to enter the city of nirvāṇa; this is what is called a "deep pit."

This refers to the deep pit of birth and death (*saṃsāra*). *Iṣīkā*—translated here as "thatch fence" (*lǐyú*)—refers to the karma and afflictions (*kleśa*) of the three realms. As for "arrogance," it means:
This refers to the conceit "I am. Regarding the five factors, they refer to the five [precepts] beginning with abstaining from killing.
Regarding the six factors, they refer to the thorough guarding of the sense faculties and so forth.
As previously stated, regarding the four reliances:
they are relying on wisdom and not on consciousness;
relying on the meaning and not on the words.
Rely on sūtras of definitive meaning, not on sūtras of provisional meaning;

rely on the Dharma, not on the person. Regarding the phrase "the body and conduct are at rest," this refers to being endowed with pliancy (*praśrabdhi*). Regarding the phrase "having already drawn near," it means...
This means being in accord with the Noble Path. Regarding the term "unsurpassed man" (*anuttara-puruṣa*):
within the Lesser Vehicle, the Buddha is called "unsurpassed" because he is an Arhat. Regarding the phrase "his mind is equal": [it refers to his equanimity].
This means that the mind of an arhat is like empty space and pure water;
it cannot be disturbed by any odors one may smell. The Tibetan version states: "It is like empty space and pure water."
His mind is like space;
even if it were smeared with sandalwood or struck by an axe,
his mind would remain equanimous toward both.
The remainder of the text is self-evident.

Regarding the statement "there is absolutely nothing herein," it means that just as there is no cyclic flow within birth and death, one likewise does not harbor greedy attachment toward nirvana. Regarding the phrase "just as, etc.," [it is explained as follows].
This means that all phenomena are established based upon names, phrases, and syllables.

Since those four fruits are all established based upon the four types of yoga, such as the spiritual lineage (*gotra*), they are used as a metaphor for names, phrases, and so forth. As for the "stage of the solitary realizer" (*pratyekabuddhabhūmi*):

This means that the four bases of yoga—lineage (*gotra*), the arousal of the thought of enlightenment (*cittotpāda*), practice (*pratipatti*), and the attainment of the fruit (*phalaprāpti*)—are the same as those of the śrāvakas.
Why, then, are five characteristics enumerated here? Answer:
This means that both abiding and practice are sites for attaining yoga; therefore, they are no different from what was stated above.
"Not delighting in clamor and bustle" refers to cultivating practices for one's own benefit. "Delighting in tranquility" refers to...

This refers to not delighting in benefiting others. As for the statement "relying on the teaching of the true Dharma and engaging in limited reflection and activity," these correspond respectively to self-benefit and the lack of benefit for others.
As for the statement "aspiring to be without a teacher," [it refers to seeking realization through one's own power].
This is due to their conduct of pride (*mānacaryā*). Regarding the term "without adversaries":

this is due to their middling faculties (*madhyendriya*), meaning that when they alone attain *bodhi*, there are no Maras or celestial beings to act as enemies. Regarding the phrase "after a hundred eons": [this refers to the time required for their practice].

This means that within each of the hundred great aeons (*mahākalpa*), one encounters the appearance of various Buddhas in the world and cultivates the six types of skillfulness (*kauśalya*). Regarding the phrase "approaching the vehicle" (*yāna-samsevā*):
this refers to the initial stage of the mind. Regarding the phrases "maturing the continuum" (*saṃtati-paripācana*) and "single-mindedness" (*ekacitta*): [these refer to subsequent stages].
This refers to the middle mind of the subsequent [stage]. Regarding the phrase "conforming to the aids to penetration" (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) and so forth, there is a question here:
the four aids to penetration comprise four types.
Why is it that only these three are mentioned here? Answer:
Because the Supreme Mundane Dharma is extremely proximate to the realization of the fruit of Stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*).

Regarding the statement "this one has not yet realized [the fruit] but claims to have attained the fruit of a śramaṇa," this refers to those who claim to have attained the second or third fruits. Regarding the statement "furthermore, there is another class [of beings]," this means that their cultivation of the path for a hundred kalpas is as previously described.
Regarding the statement "furthermore, there is another class [of beings]," [it is as follows].

This means that because they possess sharp faculties, they realize the state of *aśaikṣa* (one beyond training) all at once; whereas because these [others] possess middling or dull faculties, they realize the state of *aśaikṣa* gradually.
Thus, the text of the treatise says, "or they realize the clear observation (*abhisamaya*) of the Dharma," and so forth. As for the term "rhinoceros-like" (*khaḍgaviṣāṇakalpa*):
This reveals the meaning of being solitary and without companion. As for the subsequent mention of the "flock-moving" (vargacārin) analogy, this reveals the sense of having a group;
that is to say, a certain class of pratyekabuddha practitioners is like a flock of birds.
This is because one realizes the fruit only through cultivation;
when a solitary realizer (pratyekabuddha) cultivates this stage,
they do so by delighting in dwelling among the multitude.
At the time of attaining the fruit, ten, a hundred, or even ten million [beings] appear simultaneously;
they manifest eighteen transformations in the midst of space to benefit sentient beings. Regarding the phrase "delighting in the profound":
This refers to delighting in observing the flow with the current and against the current.
To say "delighting in observation" means observing dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) and the nature of conditions (*pratyayatā*).
To say "abiding in equanimity," and so forth, means delighting in the three gates of liberation (*trivimokṣamukha*). As for "the solitary victor" (*pratyekabuddha*):

This refers to the pratyekabuddhas themselves. Regarding the phrase "the rest and so forth," although there are differences in their dwelling, the characteristics they observe are no different from those previously mentioned. Regarding the phrase "all and so forth":
This refers to the three types of pratyekabuddhas when they enter villages or towns:
first, those who well-guard their physical deportment and correctly protect against evil conditions;
second, those who well-guard the remaining sense faculties and do not follow after forms and other objects.
Third, the well-guarding of the faculty of mind means abiding in right mindfulness. Regarding the phrase "inferior beings" and so forth:

this refers to inferior sentient beings such as those of non-Buddhist traditions; if one does not extensively manifest supernatural transformations before them, they will certainly not resolve their minds [toward awakening].
He gives clothing, food, and so forth.
By virtue of such giving, he obtains great rewards in the present life.
This concludes the hand-copied notes on the thirty-fourth fascicle of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.
